<reason>Both sides were sharp and stayed on the motion as written. B built the cleaner headline frame — the money is already frozen, so both models end with the aggressor separated from its reserves, and "indefinite custody is confiscation without the trial" — and used its Pressure Questions well, forcing A to concede that the reserves never simply go home. But A absorbed that pressure honestly and turned it: a freeze conditioned on conduct (end the aggression, remedy the harm, assets unlock) is a real difference in kind from irreversible liquidation, and it is priceable by reserve managers in a way liquidation is not. Critically, A also removed the emotional core of B's "rubble or vault" framing by pointing out that windfall income on immobilized principal can fund reconstruction now — a point B first conceded ("only the scale is contested") and then contradicted in its closing by reverting to "no cheque for the victim" and recharacterising the interest as merely a custodian's collection. A caught that inconsistency in closing. A also landed the debate's most surgical hit on symmetry: B's claim that mirror aggression judgments are harmless because no third state would recognise them fails when the retaliating court already has foreign investors' assets inside its own jurisdiction and needs no foreign enforcement. Add A's grounded observation that the actual custodians of frozen reserves skim interest but refuse principal — showing where the systemic line is drawn in practice — and A's institutional objection retains force. B's veto/endpoint pressure was genuinely strong and kept this competitive, but A gave a plausible endpoint (assets outlive regimes; successor states settle to rejoin the system) plus an immediate remedy, leaving B's central asymmetry weakened rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's handling of B's Q2 dilemma: rather than dodging, A accepted that principal stays immobilized but distinguished conditioned custody (which the aggressor itself can unlock) from irreversible liquidation, and paired it with windfall interest funding repair now — which simultaneously answered the "insurance for aggression" charge and gutted B's "rubble versus vault" framing. A's mirror-court riposte (retaliatory judgments need no foreign recognition because the assets are already onshore) was the sharpest single strike.</best_rebuttal>
